newsitem.title: THAILAND: Rerngchai in parting shot as Thai successor picked.
newsitem.headline: Rerngchai in parting shot as Thai successor picked.

text.p: Outgoing Thai central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond on Tuesday blamed his abrupt resignation on political pressure as the government swiftly named his deputy to take over the post.

"Like any human being...who is discouraged by sarcastic remarks and in order to protect my integrity and that of the Bank of Thailand, I would like to show my spirit by resigning from the governorship," Rerngchai said in a statement.
"My job so far has been strongly criticised and I faced consistent political pressure for me to leave office," he said.
As Rerngchai, a career central banker, issued his statement, the cabinet named deputy governor Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi to replace him.
Chaiyawat, 50, is another 24-year central bank veteran like Rerngchai.
Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh declined to say much about Rerngchai's exit after the cabinet meeting in northern Chiang Rai town.

"I am moved. He is an example of a man who worked for the good of the country," he said. "The transfers and removals are to create unity within the country's economic framework. If anything happens, I will be solely responsible."

Rerngchai's stout defence of his position confirmed market views that he was pressured to leave so Chavalit's government could forge ahead with its own agenda and appointees to fix an economy stumbling through its worst slump in more than a decade.
Last month, respected Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan quit after policy differences with cabinet colleagues over handling of the economy.
The cabinet on Tuesday also removed the most senior civil servant in the finance ministry, Permanent Secretary Chatumongkol Sonakul, and transferred him to an inactive position in Government House.
"It's a pity that Rerngchai had to go but the government needed to clear the decks so it can make a fresh start now that it has sought IMF assistance," said a foreign debt analyst.

The government, after initial reluctance, said this week it had enlisted International Monetary Fund (IMF) assistance to help revive the battered economy and possibly get a credit line to overcome a severe liquidity crunch.
Rerngchai was blamed for the baht's disastrous showing after it was put into a managed float on July 2 from a peg to a basket of currencies. It has lost more than 20 percent of its value.
He also faced criticism for his handling of the troubled financial sector, which has been hit by a liquidity crunch and overexposure to depressed property firms.

"The politicians were taking some unfair shots at the man (Rerngchai) but they also had reasonable criticisms of him like he waited too long to float the baht and spent a lot of national reserves in defending it," said another analyst with a foreign brokerage.
"We can only hope things can get better after this with the younger and more dynamic Chaiyawat in the saddle," he added.

Rerngchai defended himself by saying the central bank under his leadership had initiated an unprecedented number of measures to deal with Thailand's economic malaise, including the de facto devaluation of the baht on July 2.
He said the central bank proposed and won government approval on July 22 for Thailand to seek assistance from the IMF to tackle the economic woes.
"(Through these measures), the long-term process of reviving the economy and strengthening financial institutions was launched," he said.
Some of the recent central bank measures had started producing positive results including easing inflation and narrowing the current account deficit, he said.
